newsitem.title: UK: Procter & Gamble UK ad drive to boost sales.
newsitem.headline: Procter & Gamble UK ad drive to boost sales.

text.p: Procter & Gamble Co (P&G), the world's biggest advertiser, has launched an advertising push for its top washing powder, Ariel, which it hopes will increase its share of the British market, the U.S. group said on Monday.

"We own some 25 percent of the (UK) 1.0 billion pound-a-year (detergent) market and we'd be looking for this campaign to help boost our market share (of sales) by about 2-3 percentage points by September 1997," Barnabas Kossmann, marketing director of Procter & Gamble Laundry Products in Britain told Reuters at a fashion show where the campaign was launched.

P&G, which spends $3.0 billion every year on advertising worldwide, is estimated by industry sources to be investing 20 to 30 million pounds on an extensive publicity campaign which will run exclusively in Britain and Ireland.

The drive is aimed at distinguishing Ariel as the fashion industry's detergent of choice in an over-crowded marketplace, where P&G faces opposition from UK supermarkets' own-brand products and its arch-rival Unilever's Persil detergent.
"It's a very competitive battleground. We have to keep offering the consumer added value," Kossmann said.

Ariel will carry the endorsement of many high-street retailers, who say the washing powder helps to keep garments looking new. The shops will eventually include this message on the washing labels of all new clothes being sold.

The main endorser is Sears stores -- the group which owns the British fashion chains Warehouse, Miss Selfridge, Wallis and Selfridges. Other shops involved are women's fashion chain Laura Ashley, Principles for Men and Mothercare, it said.
The advertising, created by the Saatchi & Saatchi agency, will show the fashion retailers endorsing Ariel in a lengthy 80 second commercial during a prime TV viewing slot this Wednesday.
The ad also features catwalk models wearing fashionable brands -- Lee Jeans, Diesel, Converse, Kangol and Daniel Poole -- all of whom may endorse Ariel in the future, Kossmann said.
P&G would not say how much it has spent, but said the ads, going out this month on radio, TV and as posters, would be seen by some 30 million people -- about half Britain's population.
Echoing similar endorsement campaigns for P&G's Tide detergent brand in the U.S. and Canada, the firm said none of the retailers had been paid to endorse the detergent.
But the value to P&G of fashion industry backing is clear.

"Consumers have told us that the technological benefits (of a detergent) are important, but they also want the leading names in fashion to advise them on how to care for their wardrobes," Paul Polman, vice president of Procter & Gamble UK, said.
P&G expects the British market for detergents to grow by about two to three percent in the next year, Polman said.
The group first announced it was planning an endorsement campaign for Ariel in May this year.
P&G was reckoned at the time to be responding to a 25 million pound marketing drive by Unilever which aimed to make its Persil detergent more attractive to young, single-household consumers.

"There is no correlation between this campaign and what Unilever is doing with Persil. This is part of our on-going marketing strategy...We see huge opportunities (for consumer goods) in all our European markets," Polman told Reuters. --London Advertising Newsdesk +44 171 542-2792
